### 4.195 Cody's Smoked Salt

**Cody smokes his own salt, and it had never been written down anywhere in this cookbook.** Dictated 2026-09-08, and it arrived because it is **load-bearing in [§6.10 Sous Vide Brisket (Richie's Method)](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md)** — that recipe's smoke flavor comes from two places, the four-hour smoke *and* the smoked salt sitting sealed against the meat for two days, so this is an ingredient in that recipe rather than a garnish.

**What he actually said is short, and this entry is careful to keep his part separate from the cookbook's:** he uses **a thick, coarse sea salt** and smokes it for **about a couple of hours**, and **he also smokes pink Himalayan salt.** That's all of it — **the smoker temperature, the wood, and how deep to spread the salt are not his**, and every one of them is labeled below.

> 📖 **Cookbook judgment, labeled — where the missing numbers came from.** Per [CLAUDE.md §3d](../../CLAUDE.md), the gaps here were filled from this cookbook first. **[§4.115 Smoked Garlic Powder or Smoked Onion Powder](4115-smoked-garlic-powder-or-smoked-onion-powder.md) is the direct precedent** — Meathead Goldwyn's own method, in ***Meathead: The Science of Great Barbecue and Grilling***, for smoking a dry seasoning ingredient rather than a piece of meat: **a smoker at 225°F, or a grill set up two-zone, with the material spread on a grill topper or a sheet pan on the indirect side, and the smoke kept rolling for 1 to 2 hours.** **Cody's "about a couple of hours" lands exactly in that window**, which is the reason this is a reasonable source to borrow the rest from, and **225°F is also the temperature he runs on every other pit in this cookbook** ([§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md), [§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md), [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md)). **What is Cody's:** the salt, the coarseness, the pink Himalayan, and the two hours. **What is the cookbook's:** the 225°F, the indirect setup, and the thin-layer instruction in Step 2. **The day he gives his own figures, his supersede these.**

> 🧂 **Not the same thing as the store-bought hickory-smoked salt this cookbook already mentions — but they do the same job.** [§4.26 Basic Barbecue Rub](426-basic-barbecue-rub.md) (Raichlen) calls for **1 Tbsp of hickory-smoked salt** and notes on the page that it's sold in the spice rack of most supermarkets. **That's a commercial product; this is Cody's homemade version, and they're interchangeable in a pinch** — his is coarser, and he controls the wood and the depth of smoke, which a jar doesn't let you do. **Use his in §4.26 if you have it**, and use a store-bought jar in [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) if you don't, knowing that entry leans on the smoked salt harder than most recipes would.

**Techniques used:** [§T35 Smoke Science](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md) *(blue smoke, and **Cody's palmful-of-wood rule** — it applies here too)* · [§T37 Salt, Brining, and the Dry Brine](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md) *(salt types, and why grain size changes how much salt a spoonful holds)* · [§T109 Indirect Heat](t109-indirect-heat--putting-something-between-the-fire-and-the-food.md)

**Yield:** as much as your pan holds — **the figures below assume a 2-cup batch**, which is a sensible amount to make at once given it keeps indefinitely *(no quantity was given; see Open Questions)*

**🟢 Easy** · **Prep ~5 min** *(spreading the salt in a pan)* · **Slow cook ~2 hr** *(in the smoker, unattended)* · **Start to finish ~2 hr 10 min** *(plus cooling)*

**❤️ Family favorite** — *rated by Cody on 2026-09-09, in a batch of family verdicts given without a per-dish quote.*

> **Easy, and not a close call.** Nothing here can go from perfect to ruined — salt cannot overcook, burn, or break. The worst outcome is salt that tastes less smoky than you wanted, and the fix is to put it back on for another hour. *(Over-smoking is the one direction worth watching, per [§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md) — see Step 1.)*

#### A. Ingredients

- **Coarse sea salt** — **thick, coarse grains.** ✅ *Cody's own: a thick, coarse sea salt is what he smokes.* Figure **2 cups** for a batch *(the coarseness matters — see Step 2)*
- **Pink Himalayan salt** — ✅ *he smokes this too*, the same way. Coarse grind
- **Smoking wood** — **a handful, a palmful, no more** *(his standing rule, [§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md). **He didn't say which wood he uses for salt** — see Open Questions; **pecan** is his favorite across this cookbook and **hickory** is the species behind the store-bought smoked salt at [§4.26](426-basic-barbecue-rub.md))*

#### B. Cooking Instructions

**1. Get the smoker to 225°F and wait for thin blue smoke.**
**225°F, indirect** ([§T109](t109-indirect-heat--putting-something-between-the-fire-and-the-food.md)) — *this temperature is the cookbook's, borrowed from [§4.115](4115-smoked-garlic-powder-or-smoked-onion-powder.md), not Cody's; see the note above.* **A palmful of wood and no more** ([§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md)), and **let the fire settle until the smoke goes thin and blue** rather than thick and white — the bitter, acrid smoke burns off first, and salt takes on whatever you give it. **This step matters more here than it does with meat**, because there is no fat, no bark and no twelve hours of dilution to hide behind: dirty smoke on bare salt gives you bitter salt, and it doesn't cook out.

**2. Spread the salt in a shallow pan, in a thin layer, and put it on the indirect side.**
Use a **sheet pan, a disposable foil pan, or a grill topper**, and **spread the salt no more than about ¼ inch deep.** *(The thin layer is cookbook judgment, not Cody's instruction — the reasoning is [§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md)'s: **smoke only penetrates about ⅛ inch**, so a deep pile smokes its top and leaves everything underneath plain. [§4.115](4115-smoked-garlic-powder-or-smoked-onion-powder.md) spreads its garlic and onion out the same way.)* **Coarse salt is the right salt for this and fine table salt is not** — big, irregular grains have far more surface area exposed to the smoke and they don't pack down into a solid crust the way fine salt does.

**3. Smoke about two hours. Stir it once or twice along the way.**
✅ **Cody's number: about a couple of hours.** Keep the smoke rolling — thin and blue — for the full stretch. **Stir or shake the pan once or twice** so the grains that were buried get their turn on top; *that's the cookbook's addition, following from the thin-layer reasoning above, not something he specified.* **The salt will darken** — a light tan to grey-brown depending on the wood and the fire — and it will smell unmistakably of smoke while it's still warm. **Taste a few grains before you call it done**; if it's not smoky enough, put it back on. There is no way to overcook salt, so the only real judgment here is your own palate.

**4. Cool it, break up any clumps, and store it dry.**
Let the pan come to room temperature. Smoked salt often picks up a little moisture and clumps; **break the clumps up with your fingers or a fork** and put it in an **airtight jar**, out of the light. **It keeps essentially forever** — salt doesn't spoil, and the smoke compounds fade only slowly. **Label the jar**, because smoked salt looks like dirty salt and this is not a thing you want to guess at mid-recipe.

> 💡 **Do the pink Himalayan in the same load.** Cody smokes both, so if you're firing a pit for two hours anyway, run a second pan. They aren't interchangeable in every use — pink Himalayan has a slightly different mineral taste and is often sold in a coarser grind — but both take smoke the same way. *(⚠️ And per [§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md), a reminder that matters: **pink Himalayan salt is not a curing salt.** It has nothing to do with pink Prague Powder #1/#2, which contain nitrite. Don't substitute one for the other, ever.)*

> ⚖️ **Measure smoked salt by weight if you're being precise.** Coarse grains hold a lot of air, so a teaspoon of coarse smoked sea salt carries meaningfully less sodium than a teaspoon of table salt — [§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md) puts 1 tsp of Morton's kosher at about ½ tsp of table salt. **It matters most where the salt is doing real work** — [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) is seasoned by the handful and by feel, which is fine on a whole brisket; a measured recipe is a different story.

#### C. Grocery Shopping List

**🛒 General grocery**

- 🛒 **Coarse sea salt** — buy the big container; **thick, coarse grains, not fine** *(a batch is a couple of cups, and [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md) uses it heavily)*
- 🛒 **Pink Himalayan salt, coarse** — optional, and worth smoking in the same load
- 🛒 Smoking wood — **a palmful is the whole amount** *(pecan is his favorite across this cookbook; his wood for salt specifically isn't recorded — see Open Questions)*
- 🛒 Disposable foil pans, or a grill topper
- 🛒 An airtight jar, and a label

#### D. Open Questions

- **What wood does he smoke salt with?** Not recorded. **Pecan is his favorite wood everywhere else in this cookbook** ([§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md), [§6.1](61-smoked-brisket.md), [§6.9](69-codys-pulled-pork.md), [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md)), and **hickory** is what the commercial smoked salt at [§4.26](426-basic-barbecue-rub.md) is made with — but **neither is written in here as his**, because he didn't say. This is the single most useful thing to ask him about this entry, since the wood is most of the flavor.
- **What temperature does he run, and is it a hot smoke or a cold smoke?** **The 225°F in Step 1 is cookbook judgment from [§4.115](4115-smoked-garlic-powder-or-smoked-onion-powder.md), not his figure.** Worth confirming — some people cold-smoke salt at well under 100°F for much longer, which gives a different, cleaner smoke flavor, and **his two hours suggests a hot smoke**, but it isn't stated.
- **How deep does he spread it, and does he stir it?** Both are the cookbook's, reasoned from [§T35](t35-smoke-science--combustion-the-smoke-ring-and-getting-blue-smoke.md)'s ⅛-inch smoke penetration and [§4.115](4115-smoked-garlic-powder-or-smoked-onion-powder.md)'s spread-it-out method. Labeled as such in Steps 2 and 3.
- **How much does he make at a time?** No quantity was given; the entry assumes a 2-cup batch for the Nutrition block and says so.
- **Which brand or type of coarse sea salt?** He said thick and coarse, not a brand. Grain size changes how much salt a handful carries ([§T37](t37-salt-brining-and-the-dry-brine--codys-standing-practice-heavy-every-time.md)), which matters in [§6.10](610-sous-vide-brisket-richies-method.md), where the seasoning is done by feel.
- **Does he smoke anything else in the same load?** [§4.115](4115-smoked-garlic-powder-or-smoked-onion-powder.md) (smoked garlic and onion powder) and [§4.167 Smoked Butter](4167-smoked-butter.md) are both in this cookbook and both want a pit at the same temperature for the same couple of hours. Whether he runs them together is unrecorded, but it's an obvious efficiency.
